teaching.causalExplanation: The goals were agreed by national governments, but the United Nations itself points out that most of the targets can't be reached without local government. Look at what a council controls: parks, pools and lighting, footpaths and crossings, planning near schools, libraries and youth spaces, community grants, and food and water safety. So localisation means adapting the goals to local priorities, and reporting local data against them. It runs both ways. Downwards, a council asks what the goals mean here. Upwards, it reports local results, and some Australian councils publish their own review. So, the school. The fair verdict has two parts. Awareness has real value: students learned, the school signalled that these issues matter, and money went somewhere useful. But it changed nothing on the second list, and that's where its own students lose health. It treated the goals as a topic, not a tool. Awareness starts from the goals, and is measured by who turned up. Localisation starts from a local need, and is measured by change from a baseline. And labelling existing activity with goal numbers, when no decision changed, is called SDG-washing. The test is simple: would any decision have been different without the goals? Here's the method, and you start at step one, not step three. One: establish the need, with the community, and reach beyond the students already in sport or leadership. Two: name the goals it sits under, with mechanisms, not icons. Three: find the assets before the deficits: a hall, a club, a bus, a trusted organisation. Four: design across at least three Ottawa action areas, with who acts and roughly what it costs. Five: set a baseline and an indicator, reported for the groups most at risk. Six: say how it survives. The goals tell you what matters and how to measure it. The Charter tells you what kind of action to take.

scenes.teachingReason: The goals were agreed by national governments, but the United Nations itself points out that most of the targets can't be reached without local government. Look at what a council controls: parks, pools and lighting, footpaths and crossings, planning near schools, libraries and youth spaces, community grants, and food and water safety. So localisation means adapting the goals to local priorities, and reporting local data against them. It runs both ways. Downwards, a council asks what the goals mean here. Upwards, it reports local results, and some Australian councils publish their own review.

scenes.teachingReason: So, the school. The fair verdict has two parts. Awareness has real value: students learned, the school signalled that these issues matter, and money went somewhere useful. But it changed nothing on the second list, and that's where its own students lose health. It treated the goals as a topic, not a tool. Awareness starts from the goals, and is measured by who turned up. Localisation starts from a local need, and is measured by change from a baseline. And labelling existing activity with goal numbers, when no decision changed, is called SDG-washing. The test is simple: would any decision have been different without the goals?

scenes.teachingReason: It isn't localisation. No decision changed, so it's SDG-washing: a label on existing activity. To localise, start from a local need. For example, if students have nowhere quiet to study after school, extend library hours on school nights, set a baseline of student use, and report it by group. The classic mistake is counting a new label as a new action.
